In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the factors that influence the decision-making of clinicians and patients in the emergency setting.
the way in which doctors and patients make decisions about the risks and benefits of medical procedures, and the extent to which these decisions are informed by guidelines.
the way in which clinical practice guidelines are used in the real-world setting of the emergency department.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk tolerance of emergency physicians is higher for missing SAH diagnosis than neurologists and neurosurgeons.
the emergency department consultants are willing to accept a higher rate of false-negative results for the sake of a non-intrusive test.
there is no difference in risk tolerances between emergency department clinicians and neuroscience specialists.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is an urgent need to understand how clinicians perceive the risk–benefit ratio of tests in order to improve guideline adherence.

we have identified that there is a divergence of risk tolerances for SAH investigation between emergency medicine consultants and neuroscience specialists and that this is not explained by lack of familiarity with the guidelines.
we found that emergency physicians are more tolerant of missing SAH diagnosis in a patient with sudden onset headache than neuro-specialists.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a divergence between the emergency medicine and neuroscience specialists' views of risk tolerance for investigation of suspected SAH.
there are significant differences between the risk tolerances of emergency department clinicians and neuroscience specialists for investigation of suspected SAH.

there are differences in risk tolerance between emergency physicians and neuro-specialists in the investigation of spontaneous SAH, which may explain some of the observed variation in clinical practice.
